question: Delia stayed visibly distant after the rumour started. What does the scenario show about that decision?

options.text: Withdrawing support removed the one person whose backing would have ended it
options.note: She was the only one who could say "he's good, I hired him, that's the end of it." Her distance is what made that sentence unavailable for eleven weeks.

options.text: The reasoning was sound and the outcome was still harm
options.note: She isn't wrong that a public defence would have been read as confirmation. Both things are true, which is why nobody in the story is a villain and it happens anyway.

options.text: The cost landed on him and the decision was made without him
options.note: He was never told there was a strategy. He experienced it as his manager going cold on him in week six, and drew the obvious conclusion.

options.text: It was the correct call, since public defence would have made things worse
options.note: This is Delia's own position for most of the scene — right up until she hears herself say what it cost. Agreeing with her here means stopping where she stopped.

options.text: She was uncomfortable with him personally and used the rumour as cover
options.note: Nothing supports this. It's the more satisfying story because it gives you someone to blame, which is exactly why it's worth noticing you reached for it.

options.text: It had no real effect, since the rumour faded anyway
options.note: It faded and he did the migration alone, at forty percent over, because nobody would pair with him. The rumour ending isn't the same as it costing nothing.

question: His review is strong on delivery but flags "communication style" — prickly, hard to read. Why does this pattern matter?

options.text: Vague style feedback with no comparator lets bias into a formal record while sounding objective
options.note: "Prickly compared to who?" is the entire problem in three words, and the scenario has Delia fail to answer it.

options.text: It's unattributed — "the word that came back twice" names nobody he can respond to
options.note: He can't examine it, can't contest it, and can't tell whether it came from the person whose hand was on his shoulder.

options.text: It's the only part of the review that isn't measurable, and it's the part that decides the promotion
options.note: Delivery is strong and undisputed. The promotion turns on the one axis with no numbers attached.

options.text: Style feedback is never legitimate in a performance review
options.note: It often is. It needs specifics, examples and a comparator — the things this feedback doesn't have.

options.text: It matters only because the delivery numbers were good
options.note: Strong delivery makes the contrast visible. It isn't what makes the feedback a problem.

options.text: It shows his manager had decided against him from the start
options.note: She hired him and she put him on the ledger work. The chapter is about someone who was on his side and still did this.

question: Owen's idea is repeated back by Chesca and credited to her. What distinguishes ethical bystander action from private sympathy?

options.text: It happens in the room, in public, where the credit was lost
options.note: The record is public. Anything that corrects it privately leaves the record alone.

options.text: It costs the person doing it something real
options.note: Two people afterwards call him a bit intense lately. That's the price, and paying it is what separates this from a thumbs up.

options.text: It counts whether or not the person notices or thanks them
options.note: Owen doesn't thank him and probably didn't register it. It was still the thing worth doing, which is the least comfortable part of the answer.

options.text: Messaging Owen privately achieves the same outcome with less conflict
options.note: It achieves a different outcome: Owen feels seen, and the room still thinks it was Chesca's. Kind, free, and it changes nothing.

options.text: It involves reporting the incident to a manager afterwards
options.note: Linda was in the room and said "nice one, Chesca." There is no afterwards that fixes a thing that needed four seconds at the time.

options.text: It requires being more senior than the person who took the credit
options.note: He isn't senior to anyone here. He does it anyway, badly, and it still counts.

question: Delia realises mid-sentence what her distance cost him. What would a trauma-informed response look like from her at that moment?

options.text: Name what she did without asking him to absolve her
options.note: "That was me. I did that." — and then not looking at him for a response. The scenario deliberately doesn't let her apologise, because an apology would hand him a job to do.

options.text: Ask what he needs now rather than deciding for him
options.note: Her last decision on his behalf is what they're discussing. Making another one, even a generous one, repeats it.

options.text: Sit with it rather than resolving it in the room
options.note: "I'm going to have to sit with it." Nothing about this is fixable in the forty minutes, and pretending otherwise would be for her comfort.

options.text: Apologise immediately and repeatedly so he knows she is sorry
options.note: Repeated apology turns him into the person managing her guilt. He then has to say it's fine, and it isn't.

options.text: Explain the reasoning again so he understands she meant well
options.note: She has already explained it. Explaining it twice is asking him to agree the decision was reasonable, which is a request, not a repair.

options.text: Promise to fix it publicly at the next all-hands
options.note: The same instinct that started this — deciding, alone, what public gesture is good for him. Eleven weeks late and without asking.
